title: Permitted Purpose
description: Under IRC § 41(d)(3), research must aim at a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality of a business component.
summary: Permitted purpose is the federal R&D tax credit requirement under IRC § 41(d)(3) that U.S. taxpayers' research be undertaken to achieve a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component. It is applied separately to each business component, and research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors never qualifies.

body.text: Permitted purpose is the federal R&D tax credit requirement under IRC § 41(d)(3) that U.S. taxpayers' research be undertaken to achieve a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component. It is applied separately to each business component, and research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors never qualifies.

Under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4 (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4), the "Permitted Purpose" requirement—statutorily designated as a "qualified purpose" under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and IRC § 41(d)(3)(A), operating in tandem with the business component requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)—serves as the foundational substantive filter governing federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit eligibility. To qualify, a taxpayer's experimental activities must be undertaken to discover technological information whose application is intended to develop a new or improved business component specifically with respect to its function, performance, reliability, or quality, whereas IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) categorically disqualify research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

As of late 2026, substantiating Permitted Purpose carries heightened judicial and procedural consequences for U.S. taxpayers. Appellate rulings by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023) (affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15), and Moore v. Commissioner, No. 23-2681 (7th Cir. Apr. 30, 2024) (affirming T.C. Memo. 2023-20), confirm that failing to segregate qualified functional experimentation from routine commercial fabrication, aesthetic design, business management, or second-tier executive oversight ("supervision of supervision" barred under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)) results in complete disallowance of disputed Qualified Research Expenses (QREs). Simultaneously, revised IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. Dec. 2024, and Rev. Dec. 2025 Instructions released in February 2026) makes Section G (Business Component Information) mandatory for original returns for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026—absent either a qualified small business payroll tax credit election under IRC § 41(h)(3) or the small-filer exception for controlled groups with ≤$1.5 million in QREs and ≤$50 million in prior three-year average annual gross receipts—while amended-return refund claims remain governed by the three-item upfront specificity mandate under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 4.46.3.7.6 (streamlined effective June 18, 2024, with a 45-day perfection transition period extended through January 10, 2027, per IRS guidance updated October 1, 2026).
Executive Summary: The Functional Imperative of Permitted Purpose

Within the statutory architecture of the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC § 41—made permanent by the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015—the Permitted Purpose requirement, widely referred to in tax practice as the functional purpose test or business component test, functions as the primary substantive gatekeeper determining whether experimental outlays qualify for tax relief. Under IRC § 41(a)(1) and IRC § 38(b)(4), the regular research credit provides a general business credit equal to 20% of the excess of current-year QREs over a statutory base amount—or, if elected on Form 6765 Section B under IRC § 41(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9, an Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) reported in tax practice at 14% of QREs exceeding 50% of average QREs for the three preceding tax years (or 6% of current-year QREs where the taxpayer had zero QREs in any one of those three prior years). This credit delivers a dollar-for-dollar reduction in federal income tax liability—or up to $500,000 annually against employer Social Security payroll taxes for qualified small businesses electing under IRC § 41(h)—subject to IRC § 280C(c) deduction-reduction rules or a timely 21% reduced-credit election. None of these computational benefits are available, however, unless the underlying activities satisfy the statutory definition of "qualified research" in IRC § 41(d). At the heart of that definition, the Permitted Purpose test mandates that research activities be undertaken with the specific objective of discovering technological information to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Not every modification or product enhancement crosses this threshold: under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A), the intended advancement must relate directly to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component, while modifications relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors are statutorily excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B).

The strategic significance of the Permitted Purpose requirement lies in its causal role across the broader four-part statutory test for qualified research under IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a). Rather than operating as an isolated compliance checkbox, the functional objective establishes the legal and engineering boundary within which all companion statutory criteria—domestic research-and-experimental expenditure eligibility (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), reliance on principles of the hard sciences (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)), elimination of technical uncertainty (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)), and a systematic process of experimentation (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C))—must operate. When an organization fails to articulate a specific, measurable functional objective at the inception of an engineering project, subsequent design iterations lack the statutory nexus needed to substantiate in-house employee wages (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), consumed supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), eligible computer rental outlays (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii)), or contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)) as QREs.

Furthermore, because IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) requires the qualification tests to be applied separately with respect to each discrete business component of the taxpayer, businesses cannot aggregate routine post-production maintenance, aesthetic user-interface redesigns, or customer-specific adaptations into a broader innovative platform to shelter ineligible expenses. Where an overarching commercial product or system incorporates too much routine or non-functional work to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), a taxpayer's sole regulatory fallback is the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), which steps the Permitted Purpose and experimentation evaluation down to smaller discrete subcomponents—a remedial mechanism that federal courts decline to apply when taxpayers lack granular subcomponent-level records tying employee hours and technical uncertainties to those discrete subsets.
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of Permitted Purpose
The Credit for Increasing Research Activities and the Four-Part Test

Codified under 26 U.S.C. § 41, the federal R&D tax credit incentivizes domestic expenditures paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business to design, develop, or improve products, processes, computer software, techniques, formulas, or inventions. Substantive qualification is governed by the four-part test of IRC § 41(d) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 (Qualified research for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), reinforced procedurally by heightened component-level reporting mandates on IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities).

Under the verbatim text of the Internal Revenue Code, IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) does not house the technological-in-nature requirement; instead, it establishes the threshold Section 174A / Section 174 expenditure test. Through the 2024 taxable year, IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) required research "with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under section 174", incorporating the Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 standard that costs represent research and development in the experimental or laboratory sense aimed at eliminating uncertainty. On July 4, 2025, Congress enacted the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21), restoring immediate deductibility for domestic research and experimental expenditures under newly added IRC § 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (while retaining mandatory 15-year amortization under IRC § 174 for foreign research), and made a conforming amendment to 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), which now requires research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A" (while existing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i) still cross-references section 174 and § 1.174-2 pending conforming regulatory amendments).

The remaining statutory clauses of IRC § 41(d)(1) and IRC § 41(d)(3) then interact to establish technological nature, technical uncertainty, business component usefulness, experimentation, and Permitted Purpose. Specifically, IRC § 41(d)(1)(B) requires research "undertaken for the purpose of discovering information— (i) which is technological in nature, and (ii) the application of which is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer". Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken to "discover information" if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability or method for developing or improving a business component, or the appropriate design of that component, while Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) defines "technological in nature" as fundamental reliance on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Finally, IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) requires research "substantially all of the activities of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in paragraph (3)". Paragraph (3)—IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)—defines those qualifying purposes exclusively as relating to (i) a new or improved function, (ii) performance, or (iii) reliability or quality, while IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) mandates that research "shall in no event be treated as conducted for a purpose described in this paragraph if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors", a rule codified in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) under the regulatory heading "Qualified purpose". In tax practice and IRS audit guidance, practitioners combine IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) (new or improved business component) with IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)–(B) (qualified functional purpose) as the operational Permitted Purpose prong, while pairing IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (Section 174A / 174 experimental outlays) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) as the Elimination of Uncertainty prong.

headers: Substantive Requirement Related to Permitted Purpose

cells: Permitted Purpose (Business Component & Qualified Purpose)

Research must be intended to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a discrete business component; research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors is statutorily excluded.
Pre-project technical charters, quantitative performance specifications, baseline capability gap analyses, and engineering failure criteria.
Elimination of Uncertainty (Section 174A / Discovering Information)
Domestic R&E activities must aim to discover information eliminating technical uncertainty as to capability, method, or appropriate design required to achieve the Permitted Purpose.
Technical hypotheses, documented baseline engineering knowledge gaps, and architectural or metallurgical feasibility assessments.
Technological in Nature

The experimental process used to discover information and achieve the functional improvement must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.
Hard-science principles, mathematical/engineering calculations, software algorithms, and technical disciplines utilized.
Process of Experimentation

Substantially all (≥80%) of the research activities per business component must constitute elements of an evaluative process (modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error) evaluating alternatives to achieve the Permitted Purpose.
Prototype test logs, iterative design revisions, version-control (git) commit histories, simulation outputs, and technical failure debriefs.

body.text: Causal Interdependence and the Substantially All Requirement

The four prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1) operate as an integrated causal chain rather than detached compliance criteria. The Permitted Purpose (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(3)(A)) defines the destination of the research effort—the specific functional capability, processing benchmark, or structural reliability standard sought. Technical uncertainty (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)) represents the engineering obstacle preventing immediate realization of that functional goal using information available to the taxpayer at project outset. Notably, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) codifies an important operational nuance in this chain: a taxpayer may validly undertake a process of experimentation even if there is no uncertainty regarding its capability or method of achieving the desired functional result, so long as the appropriate design of that result is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. However, the same regulation cautions that design uncertainty alone does not establish that all activities undertaken to build the business component constitute a process of experimentation; rather, the activities must identify one or more technical alternatives and systematically evaluate them using principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4), (a)(5)(i)).

Treasury Regulations enforce this causal interdependence through the quantitative "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6). Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the substantially all requirement is satisfied only if 80% or more (≥80%) of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, and determined without regard to the separate 80% employee-level wage rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2)—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose described in IRC § 41(d)(3).

As practitioner analyses of the regulatory fraction explain, this 80% standard functions as a binary component-level cliff. Where at least 80% of the research activities on a business component constitute elements of an experimental process aimed at a Permitted Purpose (such as developing a new function), the component satisfies IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), and remaining research activities up to the 20% margin (such as product styling activities that otherwise meet IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and do not violate an express exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)) do not disqualify the component. Conversely, Permitted Purpose cannot be a peripheral or incidental byproduct of an initiative predominantly aimed at organizational restructuring, workflow optimization, routine fabrication, or commercial customization. If non-functional, managerial, or aesthetic activities push the experimental numerator of the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction below 80%, the entire overall business component fails the substantially all threshold, disqualifying all associated expenditures unless a qualifying subcomponent can be isolated under the shrinking-back rule.
Disaggregation and the Business Component Rule

Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), a "business component" encompasses any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be (i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. While this six-category definition spans tangible hardware and intangible software or chemical formulations alike, its application is strictly bounded by IRC § 41(d)(2)(A), which mandates that IRC § 41(d)(1) "shall be applied separately with respect to each business component of the taxpayer". In addition, IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) sets forth a special rule for production processes, reinforced by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), under which activities relating to the development of a manufacturing or other commercial production process are evaluated separately from activities relating to the development of the underlying product itself.

This component-by-component evaluation rule prevents the cross-subsidization of routine commercial engineering costs by genuinely innovative R&D. For example, in a hypothetical product development initiative encompassing both the synthesis of a novel chemical formula and the design of standard commercial packaging for that formula, IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) applies the Permitted Purpose test independently to the chemical formulation and to the packaging component. Even where the chemical formula satisfies all four prongs of IRC § 41(d)(1), routine packaging development that relies on established materials, predictable structural parameters, or visual shelf-appeal graphics (IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)) fails the Permitted Purpose and technical uncertainty tests, requiring its associated wage and supply costs to be segregated and excluded from QREs. Conversely, under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), even after the chemical formula meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements for sale, experimental engineering undertaken to develop a novel manufacturing process for that formula can qualify independently as its own separate "process" business component if the process development separately satisfies IRC § 41(d).

Where an integrated commercial product (such as a complete vessel, industrial machine, or multi-module software platform) fails the Permitted Purpose or 80% experimentation requirement at the overall product level, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) provides the shrinking-back rule. Under this rule, the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) are reapplied first at the level of the discrete subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention, stepping downward iteratively until either a subset of elements satisfies the four-part test (including its own Permitted Purpose and 80% substantially all threshold) or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails. Federal case law confirms that the shrinking-back rule applies solely when the overall business component fails IRC § 41(d)(1)—not as a government mechanism to exclude research activities once an overall component qualifies—but taxpayers can invoke shrinking-back protection only if their accounting and engineering records disaggregate activities and costs to the specific qualifying subcomponent.
Mechanics of Functional Improvement and Practical Application
Quantifying Functional Advancement Versus Aesthetic Modification

To withstand IRS examination, a claimed Permitted Purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) should be framed in objective, quantifiable engineering metrics establishing a clear technical advancement over the taxpayer's existing baseline. Vague qualitative aspirations—such as "creating a better product," "modernizing the platform," or "improving operational workflow"—fail to demonstrate a statutory functional purpose because they describe general commercial or managerial goals rather than measurable advances in function, performance, reliability, or quality. Instead, defensible claims anchor the Permitted Purpose in concrete technical parameters—such as illustrative hypothetical benchmarks targeting a +35% increase in processing throughput, a component failure rate below 0.05%, or a -40% reduction in computational query latency under peak load conditions.

At the same time, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) clarifies that pursuing a Permitted Purpose and discovering technological information does not require the taxpayer to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering. Likewise, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) confirms that a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on established principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy the technological-in-nature requirement, provided genuine baseline uncertainty exists within the taxpayer's own development effort—though Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 cautions that merely employing computers or information technology to store, collect, manipulate, translate, disseminate, or process data does not by itself establish qualified research.

Equally critical is the statutory boundary in IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) separating functional improvements from aesthetic, style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design modifications. This functional-versus-ornamental divide is mirrored directly in the Patent Safe Harbor of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii): while issuance of a utility patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under 35 U.S.C. § 151 constitutes conclusive evidence that a taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning a business component, the regulation explicitly carves out design patents issued under 35 U.S.C. § 171 because design patents protect ornamental appearance rather than functional utility. Across engineering disciplines, the decisive analytical question is why the technical modification is pursued and what physical, chemical, biological, or computational property it alters. In software engineering, re-architecting a database query engine to achieve an illustrative 40% reduction in peak-load latency directly advances system performance and reliability under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)(ii)–(iii), whereas redesigning the user-interface dashboard layout and updating the color palette to align with corporate branding is an excluded aesthetic activity under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). In polymer manufacturing, engineering an injection-molding thermal control process to reduce part warping and dimensional rejection rates by an illustrative 15% targets quality and reliability, whereas altering the surface texture of a plastic housing solely to impart a "more premium" tactile feel without structural benefit fails as a style-driven modification—just as custom architectural building moldings and decorative paint renovations have been disallowed in administrative tax rulings under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Similarly, in food science, formulating a novel preservative blend that doubles product shelf life from an illustrative 6 months to 12 months without degrading flavor stability constitutes a qualifying performance and quality improvement, whereas modifying a food dye formulation so a snack appears a "spicier" shade of red is excluded as a cosmetic or preference-driven adjustment.
Distinguishing Experimental Research from Routine Quality Control

A core regulatory function of the Permitted Purpose criterion, operating alongside IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v), is to filter out ordinary manufacturing operations, routine engineering adjustments, and standard quality control (QC) verification. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(D)(v), "routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control" is expressly excluded from qualified research. Activities conducted for routine regulatory compliance verification, batch release inspection, or standard quality assurance fail both IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v) and the Permitted Purpose standard because their objective is to verify adherence to pre-existing specifications rather than to discover technological information resolving uncertainty over a new or improved functional capability.

The distinction between excluded QC testing and qualifying experimental validation turns on the state of baseline technical uncertainty and the engineering purpose of the evaluation. Testing a completed commercial unit at the end of an assembly line to verify that it meets established manufacturing tolerances is an excluded routine QC activity under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v). Conversely, placing trial prototypes composed of candidate materials and varying wall thicknesses into an accelerated environmental test chamber and performing destructive cross-sectional testing to determine how deeply corrosive stresses penetrate—as illustrated in IRS Amended Return FAQ 20—is an integral part of a Process of Experimentation (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)) aimed at resolving technical uncertainty for a Permitted Purpose. Treasury Regulations draw a parallel functional boundary in pharmaceutical development under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv): clinical testing prior to U.S. commercial production is not treated as post-production research even if the drug is commercially available in other countries, and additional clinical testing conducted after Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval escapes the post-commercial-production exclusion only when undertaken to establish a new functional use, characteristic, indication, combination, dosage, or delivery form that must itself be approved by the FDA.
Hypothetical Comparative Analysis: Aerospace Process Engineering Versus Client Adaptation

In a qualifying advanced aerospace material engineering scenario, a domestic manufacturing enterprise initiates a project to develop a new metal alloy component (a discrete "product" business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) for commercial aircraft engines. At project inception, the technical lead defines the Permitted Purpose as increasing the component's maximum continuous operating temperature tolerance by an illustrative +250°C above the threshold of existing commercially available alloys, directly targeting improvements in engine thermal performance and structural reliability under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)(ii)–(iii). Because existing metallurgical formulations cannot sustain a 250°C thermal increase without structural degradation, this functional objective immediately creates baseline technical uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) regarding both the chemical formulation (capability and appropriate design) and the thermal mixing process (method). The engineering team's subsequent work—formulating candidate alloys, designing specialized mixing apparatus, running extreme thermal simulations, casting experimental pilot models (defined under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) as models of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during development or improvement), and destructively testing prototypes to measure thermal tolerances—constitutes a qualifying process of experimentation driven directly by the Permitted Purpose. Even if prototype testing ultimately achieves only an illustrative +180°C improvement and management terminates the project because the full +250°C target proves metallurgically unattainable, the incurred domestic IRC § 174A outlays still satisfy the Permitted Purpose test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), because eligibility turns on systematic experimental effort directed at resolving technical uncertainty for a functional advance rather than achieving commercial completion.

By contrast, in a non-qualifying client-specific machinery recalibration scenario, an engineering firm is contracted to modify a client's existing industrial manufacturing line so that the machinery can process a slightly higher volume of raw material required under a new customer supply agreement. The machinery's operational parameters and mechanical load limits are already established within standard engineering tables, and the modification consists of predictable recalibrations and minor mechanical part swaps. This activity fails qualification on two independent statutory grounds. First, because known engineering parameters already establish capability, method, and appropriate design, the work relies on routine engineering optimization without baseline technical uncertainty under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) or an evaluative process of experimentation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i). Second, the work is expressly excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3) as research related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. Taxpayers should note an important nuance in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3): this customer-adaptation exclusion "does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer", meaning custom-engineered, first-of-kind systems resolving genuine technical uncertainty can still satisfy Permitted Purpose (provided they are not disqualified as funded research), whereas customizing an existing vessel or machine design to meet a buyer's specifications—such as the Hurley Dredge modifications rejected under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) in Trinity Industries—is statutorily barred.
Statutory Exclusions and the Internal Use Software Standard
Express Exclusions Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)

Even where technical personnel perform sophisticated engineering tasks, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c) enumerate eight express categories of activities that are statutorily excluded from qualified research because their underlying objective is post-production maintenance, customer-specific customization, replication, administrative management, foreign execution, non-technological inquiry, or third-party contract fulfillment rather than proprietary domestic functional innovation.

Among these commercial exclusions, Funded Research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(H)) requires rigorous contract-by-contract legal scrutiny. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9), funded-research determinations are governed by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3) (cross-referencing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)), under which all agreements (not solely formal research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and third parties or governmental entities are evaluated across two cumulative legal requirements. First, under the payment-contingency prong (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)), amounts payable under an agreement are not treated as funding only if payment is contingent on the success of the research and thus considered paid for the product or result of the research rather than for the performance of research services regardless of outcome; if the contractor is paid on a time-and-materials or non-contingent basis regardless of technical success, the research is funded and ineligible. Second, under the substantial-rights prong (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3))—strictly enforced by the Tax Court in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1—if a taxpayer performing research for another party retains no substantial rights in the research under the governing agreement (for example, conferring exclusive exploitation rights on the customer or requiring the researcher to pay to use the results, with incidental experience or general skill gains expressly excluded from counting as substantial rights), the research is treated as fully funded and none of the contractor's outlays qualify. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) also establishes a "whipsaw" rule: if the researcher retains no substantial rights AND payments to the researcher are contingent on technical success, neither the researcher (barred under § 1.41-4A(d)(2)) nor the customer paying for the work (barred under § 1.41-2(e)(2) because contingent payments purchase a product rather than contract research) is entitled to treat any portion of the expenditures as qualified. Even where a contractor retains substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), non-contingent third-party payments still reduce otherwise qualified expenses dollar-for-dollar to the extent of the funding received.

headers: Mechanism of Permitted Purpose / Qualification Failure

cells: Post-Commercial Production Research
Once a business component is ready for commercial sale or use or meets basic functional and economic requirements, the initial Permitted Purpose has been achieved.

Subsequent debugging, minor maintenance patches, and routine production engineering must be excluded unless a separate manufacturing-process project (§ 41(d)(2)(C)) or distinct next-generation functional upgrade is initiated (or qualifying FDA clinical trials under § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv)).
Adaptation to Customer Requirements
Customizing an existing product or process to fit a specific client's operational environment serves commercial deployment rather than general functional advancement.

Client onboarding engineering, site-specific parameter tuning, and bespoke interface configurations are excluded—though custom-ordered components remain eligible if resolving genuine technical uncertainty for a new or improved capability.
Duplication of Existing Components

Reproducing an existing business component (in whole or part) from physical examination, plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or public information seeks replication rather than functional advancement.

Reverse engineering or cloning existing market functionality is excluded, though § 1.41-4(c)(4) clarifies that merely examining an existing component while developing one's own improved component does not trigger the exclusion.
Surveys, Management, Market & QC Studies

Efficiency surveys ((i)), management functions/techniques ((ii)), market research, testing, or promotions ((iii)), routine data collection ((iv)), and ordinary QC testing/inspection ((v)) lack a hard-science technological purpose.
Organizational workflow optimization, business process re-engineering, consumer market studies, and routine QA/QC inspection hours must be segregated and excluded.
Internal Use Software (Presumptive Bar)
Software developed primarily for internal general and administrative (G&A) functions lacks external product development risk unless heightened innovation criteria are met.

Presumptively excluded unless used directly in qualified research (§ 41(d)(4)(E)(i)), used in a qualifying production process ((E)(ii)), developed for third-party interaction (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)), or satisfying the three-part High Threshold of Innovation test (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)).
Foreign Research & Non-Hard Sciences
Research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions ((F)) or in the social sciences, arts, or humanities ((G)) falls outside domestic technological R&D policy.
Foreign employee or overseas contractor activities (subject to 15-year IRC § 174 amortization) and behavioral, economic, or artistic studies are ineligible.
Funded Research
Research funded by grant, contract, or otherwise where payment is not contingent on technical success or where the taxpayer retains no substantial rights in the resulting research.

Non-contingent payment contracts or IP clauses stripping substantial rights treat the engagement as excluded third-party contract fulfillment (with a mutual disallowance whipsaw under § 1.41-4A(d)(2) if contingent payment pairs with no substantial rights).

body.text: Internal Use Software and the High Threshold of Innovation Test

Software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use is governed by the Code's most stringent statutory filter under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and final Treasury Regulations issued in T.D. 9786 (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(6), promulgated October 3, 2016). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(A)–(B), software is classified as Internal Use Software (IUS) if it is developed for use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business (including software developed primarily for a related party treated as a single taxpayer under IRC § 41(f)). Final regulations strictly confine G&A functions to three operational categories: (1) financial management functions under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1) (such as accounts payable/receivable, inventory management, budgeting, cash management, cost accounting, economic forecasting, financial reporting, fixed asset and general ledger accounting, internal audit, risk management, strategic business planning, and tax); (2) human resources management functions under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(2) (such as recruiting, hiring, training, assigning personnel, personnel records, payroll, and benefits); and (3) support services under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3) that support day-to-day operations (such as data processing, facility services including groundskeeping, janitorial, and logistics, graphic services, marketing, legal services, government compliance, printing, and security services).

Before applying the heightened IUS test, taxpayers must evaluate the statutory exemptions and regulatory carve-outs reflected in the four software classifications on Section G, Line 49(e) of IRS Form 6765. First, under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E)(i)–(ii), software is statutorily excepted from IUS treatment (Form 6765 Category D) if developed for use in an activity that itself constitutes qualified research or for internal use in a production process meeting the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1). Second, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv), software is Non-IUS (Category C, evaluated solely under the standard Four-Part Test) if developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system—such as customer-facing online ordering or photo-processing portals (whereas § 1.41-4(c)(6) Example 6 specifies that software interacting with vendors for inventory management remains G&A IUS because vendors are not treated as third parties for G&A exclusion purposes). Third, for enterprise systems serving both back-office G&A functions and customer-facing functions, T.D. 9786 introduced Dual Function Software (DFS, Category B) under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi), enabling taxpayers to isolate distinct third-party-facing subsets under the standard Four-Part Test or apply a regulatory safe-harbor alternative where dual-use elements remain intertwined.

Because routine enterprise IT implementations and off-the-shelf ERP integrations do not represent the technological risk Congress intended to subsidize, software classified as G&A Internal Use Software (Category A) without an applicable exemption is eligible under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(i) only if it satisfies both the standard Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d)(1) and all three prongs of the elevated "High Threshold of Innovation" test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). Under the first prong (Innovative), the software must be intended to be innovative, meaning development is designed to achieve a reduction in cost, improvement in speed, or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant if the development is or would have been successful—elevating the Permitted Purpose well beyond an ordinary functional enhancement. Under the second prong (Significant Economic Risk, including Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C)), the software development must involve significant economic risk, whereby the taxpayer commits substantial resources and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources will be recovered within a reasonable period. Notably, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) mandates a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk for IUS than the standard uncertainty required for non-IUS business components, focusing on technical uncertainty at project inception regarding whether the final result can be achieved within a timeframe allowing recovery of substantial committed resources within a reasonable period. Under the third prong (Not Commercially Available), the software cannot be commercially available for use by the taxpayer—meaning it cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements. Furthermore, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(D) specifies that this evaluation accounts solely for results anticipated from the new or improved software itself at the outset of development (independent of concurrent hardware or other software changes) and clarifies that implementing existing technology by itself is not evidence of innovation unless using existing technology in new ways resolves substantial technical uncertainty.
Documentation, Substantiation, and Audit Defense
Contemporaneous Evidence and the IRS Audit Technique Guide

Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) (Recordkeeping for the research credit), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 "must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit". Consequently, the legal validity of a claimed Permitted Purpose is bounded by the contemporaneous documentation linking the stated functional objective to the actual experimental activities performed and the in-house wages, supplies, computer leasing costs, and contract research outlays (generally 65% of eligible third-party payments, or 75% for qualified research consortia and 100% for eligible energy research) claimed under IRC § 41(b). Under the official IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 (June 2005), together with the Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) and industry-specific guides (Aerospace [Jan. 2005], Software Process of Experimentation [May 2005], and Pharmaceuticals, Publication 5931 [Rev. April 2024]), examining agents focus intensely on nexus—requesting reconciled listings of all claimed employees with full names, job titles, cost centers, and assigned business components, while cautioning that eligibility depends strictly on what an employee actually does during a specific period rather than job titles or descriptions alone. Furthermore, the RCCATG instructs examiners that judgmental samples lack legal authority; unless a taxpayer follows formal statistical sampling procedures under Revenue Procedure 2011-42, credits are allowed strictly on individually substantiated components and expenses.

In examining wage QREs, IRS agents audit employee activities across the three statutory categories of "qualified services" defined in IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3). First, engaging in qualified research (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1)) covers the actual hands-on conduct of qualified research, such as a scientist conducting laboratory experiments or an engineer executing experimental simulations. Second, direct supervision (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)) means strictly the "immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research"—enforced in audit practice as the "one-up" rule—which excludes supervision by higher-level managers or executives to whom first-line managers report, even when those senior officers are trained scientists or engineers. Third, direct support (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)) covers services directly supporting persons engaging in actual conduct of qualified research or their immediate first-line supervisors—such as a machinist machining a prototype part, a laboratory worker cleaning research equipment, or a clerk compiling research test data—while excluding general administrative services (payroll, accounting, HR, janitorial, or corporate financial oversight) regardless of whether those staff sit inside the R&D department. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), wages of mixed-duty personnel are allocated by the ratio of hours spent on qualified services to total hours worked, with 100% wage inclusion permitted only where an individual employee's qualified services reach at least 80% of total annual services (a wage calculation rule distinct from the component-level 80% experimentation rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)).

Reconstructed post-hoc narratives, uncorroborated percentage estimates, or generalized oral testimony collected years after the tax year under examination are routinely rejected when unsupported by contemporaneous records. Substantiating Permitted Purpose requires preserving a multi-layered documentary trail generated organically across the engineering lifecycle. At project initiation, engineering requirement documents, project charters, technical hypotheses, and architectural specifications must define the functional baseline ("Current State"), the technical knowledge gap (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)), and the specific quantitative target in function, performance, reliability, or quality ("Permitted Purpose" under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)) prior to experimentation. Throughout experimental execution, iterative technical artifacts—including prototype test logs, simulation outputs, destructive failure analysis reports, design iteration histories, laboratory notes, and software version-control records such as git commit logs—must corroborate systematic evaluation of alternatives to overcome technical uncertainty. Finally, payroll and time-segregation records—including payroll registers, organizational charts verifying "one-up" supervisory chains, project calendars, and granular time-tracking logs—must segregate hours spent on functional experimentation from hours spent on excluded activities such as cosmetic UI styling (IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)), customer adaptation (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)), routine QC inspection (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v)), and post-production maintenance (IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)).
Judicial Precedent and Upfront Disclosure Mandates

Appellate litigation and IRS filing reforms between 2021 and 2026 underscore that component-level substantiation failures are fatal to R&D tax credit claims even where genuine commercial engineering took place. In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (Feb. 11, 2021), aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. Mar. 7, 2023), both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit upheld the complete disallowance of research credits claimed for a shipbuilding subsidiary (CIS) developing a tank barge (Project 720, built under contract with Apex Oil) and a drydock. The courts rejected the taxpayer's "novelty" shortcut—which sought to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) based on the proportion of newly designed physical elements of the vessels—holding that § 1.41-4(a)(6) measures research activities, not physical components, and that direct-support production fabrication and raw vessel supplies cannot enter the experimentation numerator unless the taxpayer proves the vessel or discrete subcomponent was constructed as a genuine pilot model under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) specifically to evaluate and resolve technical uncertainty. Because the taxpayer lacked subcomponent-level documentation proving that at least 80% of activities on any discrete subset constituted experimentation for a Permitted Purpose, the courts could not apply the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), resulting in total disallowance of the credit. Similarly, in Scott Moore and Gayla Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, aff'd, No. 23-2681 (7th Cir. Apr. 30, 2024), the Tax Court and Seventh Circuit disallowed the entire 65% salary-and-bonus QRE allocation claimed for Gary Robert, the President and Chief Operating Officer of scoreboard manufacturer Nevco, Inc. Even though witnesses corroborated that Robert spent 50% to 65% of his time on "new product development" and was a named inventor on a patent, the courts held that commercial "new product development" is far broader than statutory "qualified research"—encompassing market research, aesthetic design, administrative planning, and customer feedback, none of which qualify under IRC § 41(d). Without written time records under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) to establish "was it qualified?" and "how much?", and because Robert was "two layers removed" from the research engineers (supervising the Director of Engineering rather than providing immediate "one-up" supervision under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)), the taxpayers failed their burdens of production and persuasion.

Alongside these appellate rulings, the procedural framework governing upfront disclosure has evolved into two distinct administrative regimes—one governing amended-return refund claims following Harper v. United States and the other governing original income tax returns on revised IRS Form 6765. In Harper v. United States, 2019 WL 1877185 (S.D. Cal. 2019), a California federal district court dismissed a contractor's R&D refund suit ($437,632 for 2008 and $388,325 for 2010) for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under the specificity requirement of Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) because the amended returns failed to identify specific business components or set forth foundational facts establishing the exact basis of the claim. Although the Ninth Circuit reversed that dismissal based on the case-specific audit record in Harper v. United States, 847 F. App'x 408 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021), IRS Chief Counsel issued Field Attorney Advice (FAA) 20214101F (Oct. 15, 2021), maintaining the district court's specificity standard and instituting a mandatory five-item upfront disclosure rule effective January 10, 2022. Crucially, effective June 18, 2024 (codified in IRM 4.46.3.7.6 and IRS Amended Return FAQ 21), the IRS waived two of those initial submission items—eliminating the upfront requirement to list the names of individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover at the time of filing—so that a valid R&D refund claim on an amended return (or Administrative Adjustment Request for a BBA partnership) must now provide three minimum items signed under penalties of perjury: (1) identify all IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) business components forming the factual basis of the claim; (2) for each business component, identify all research activities performed (describing what the taxpayer did and how they did it); and (3) provide total qualified employee wage, supply, and contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be reported via Form 6765, including Column 49(f)). Per IRS guidance updated October 1, 2026, the transition period granting taxpayers 45 days to perfect a deficient refund claim (after receiving Letter 6426C or Letter 6428) has been extended through January 10, 2027, though employee-level and Permitted Purpose substantiation remains fully examinable upon audit.

On timely filed original tax returns, revised IRS Form 6765 (Rev. Dec. 2024, and Rev. Dec. 2025 Instructions released in February 2026) enforces upfront component-level accountability through Section G (Business Component Information, Columns 49(a)–56)—which notably does not require narrative prose describing "information sought to be discovered" or Permitted Purpose essays on the return itself. Optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (including 2025 original returns), Section G becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (on or after January 1, 2026) for all filers except (1) qualified small businesses under IRC § 41(h)(3) checking the box on Form 6765 to elect the payroll tax credit, and (2) original-return filers with controlled-group QREs (Line 48) of ≤$1.5 million AND prior three-year average annual gross receipts (under IRC § 448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph (A)) of ≤$50 million. Non-exempt filers must follow the "80% / Top 50" rule, listing business components in descending order of QREs until covering at least 80% of total QREs up to a maximum of 50 business components (with remaining components reported on an "Aggregate Business Components" line, alongside special rules for the ASC 730 Directive and Rev. Proc. 2011-42 statistical samples labeled "sample"). For each itemized component, taxpayers must disclose the conducting entity's EIN (Column 49(a)), Principal Business Activity code (49(b)), business component name or unique alphanumeric identifier matching books and records (49(c)), simplified component type (49(d): Product, Process, or All Others), software classification if applicable (49(e): A. IUS, B. DFS, C. Non-IUS, or D. Excepted from IUS treatment), and disaggregated QRE dollars split across direct-conduct wages (Column 50), direct-supervision wages (Column 51), direct-support wages (Column 52), total wages (Column 53), supplies (Column 54), computer rental/lease (Column 55), and contract research expenses (Column 56). Consequently, business component boundaries, IUS software classifications, and three-tier wage allocations can no longer be retrofitted during an IRS audit; they must be captured contemporaneously and locked into annual return preparation.

body.text: Treatment of Failed and Abandoned Research Projects

A frequent misconception in R&D tax compliance is that a research project must achieve commercial deployment or meet its targeted engineering specifications to satisfy the Permitted Purpose test. Treasury Regulations explicitly refute this assumption: 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) provides that "a determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature does not require that the taxpayer succeed in developing a new or improved business component". Similarly, for Internal Use Software, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) measures whether the software is intended to achieve a substantial and economically significant improvement "if the development is or would have been successful". Eligibility under IRC § 41(d) turns on prospective functional intent and systematic experimental effort undertaken to resolve technical uncertainty when domestic IRC § 174A expenditures are incurred, not ultimate commercial or technical success.

When an engineering project is abandoned or canceled because the technical team cannot overcome a scientific or engineering obstacle—for instance, when iterative pilot models repeatedly fail to operate within required thermal or latency tolerances despite systematic testing—the substantiated QREs remain eligible in full for the research credit. Indeed, as judicial analyses of pilot-model construction in Little Sandy Coal emphasize, technical failure severe enough to force a taxpayer to scrap a prototype and start over provides strong objective corroboration that genuine baseline uncertainty existed at the outset of the project. Conversely, if a project is terminated prior to technical evaluation purely due to non-technical commercial factors—such as shifting consumer style preferences, corporate budget cuts, or executive restructuring—IRS examiners closely scrutinize whether claimed pre-cancellation outlays were genuinely incurred in an evaluative process of experimentation (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)) rather than preliminary business planning or excluded market research (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(iii)). Maintaining contemporaneous failure debriefs that document the specific technical hurdles responsible for project cancellation is therefore essential to defending QRE eligibility on abandoned initiatives.
Strategic Governance Framework for Continuous Permitted Purpose Compliance

Operationalizing the statutory, judicial, and Form 6765 Section G demands of the Permitted Purpose test requires embedding tax compliance checkpoints directly into corporate engineering and product development workflows. Relying on year-end retrospective interviews exposes taxpayers to severe audit disallowance risk under Little Sandy Coal and Moore whenever technical leads cannot substantiate pre-project baseline capability gaps, isolate subcomponent boundaries for shrinking-back defense, or segregate non-qualifying commercial hours. Three integrated institutional governance protocols establish continuous audit readiness:

items: Mandatory Pre-Project Technical Charter Protocol: Organizations should require a standardized, contemporaneous project charter for all R&D initiatives exceeding a defined capital or payroll expenditure threshold prior to resource deployment. Authored by the first-line technical lead at project inception, this charter must assign a unique alphanumeric Business Component Identifier reconciling to corporate books and Form 6765 Section G, Column 49(c); classify the discrete component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) and Column 49(d) (Product, Process, or All Others); verify domestic U.S. execution under IRC § 174A and IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); document the baseline capability, method, or design uncertainty ("Current State" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i)); and state quantifiable target metrics in function, performance, reliability, or quality ("Permitted Purpose" under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)).

Cross-Functional Tax-Informed Technical Review Board: Corporations developing multi-subsystem hardware or enterprise software should establish a quarterly review board uniting R&D engineering directors, tax counsel, legal/contract reviewers, and financial controllers. Prior to major resource deployment, this board should formally delineate component and subcomponent boundaries to preserve Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back eligibility and IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) manufacturing-process separation; vet third-party and government contracts against Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(3) to confirm technical-success payment contingency and retention of substantial rights; and classify every software initiative across Form 6765 Column 49(e) categories (A. IUS, B. DFS, C. Non-IUS, or D. Excepted), recording formal board minutes substantiating all three prongs of the High Threshold of Innovation test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii) for any G&A Internal Use Software.

Three-Tier Activity-Based Time and Cost Segregation Architecture: Engineering time-tracking and sprint-tracking architectures must transition from broad department cost centers to contemporaneous tracking by both Business Component Identifier and Qualified Service Classification, mapping directly to IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), and Form 6765 Section G Columns 50, 51, and 52 (Direct Conduct, First-Line "One-Up" Direct Supervision, and Direct Support). By requiring engineers and first-line supervisors to differentiate hours spent on qualifying experimental activities (hypothesis modeling, simulation, pilot-model testing, and algorithmic latency optimization) from excluded task codes—specifically UI cosmetic styling (IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)), customer-specific adaptation (IRC § 41(d)(4)(B)), routine QC inspection (IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v)), post-production maintenance (IRC § 41(d)(4)(A)), and higher-tier executive oversight barred under Moore—corporations protect the 80% "substantially all" threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) on a component-by-component basis and maintain an immediately auditable trail for Form 6765 Section G and IRM 4.46.3.7.6 disclosures.
